meta.chapterLabel: Lesson 3: Asking the Time: What Time Is It?

items.note: みせ (mise) means 'restaurant/shop' on its own (sub-entry under みせの (mise no) ひと (hito), restaurant employee)
ひと (hito) means 'person' on its own (sub-entry under みせの (mise no) ひと (hito), restaurant employee)

みせの (mise no) + ひと (hito) follows the same [owner] の [thing] pattern as のぞみデパートのたなかさん (Nozomi Depaato no Tanaka-san) from Lesson 1 - here の (no) marks affiliation with the shop rather than personal possession.

items.reviewNote: Source spelling appears to be missing ン (likely a typo/OCR artifact for ランチタイム, 'lunchtime')

items.note: なんじ (nanji, 'what time') asks for a specific clock time, e.g. なんじですか (nanji desu ka), 'what time is it?' — contrast the broader いつ (itsu, 'when'), which asks about a date or time in general rather than an exact hour.
Marks a starting point in time or place ('from'); pairs with まで (made, 'until') to state a range, as in しごとはくじからごじまでです (shigoto wa kuji kara goji made desu), 'work is from 9:00 to 5:00.'

Suffix — attaches after an hour to mean 'half past' (written 〜はん (han) in the source). さんじはん (sanjihan, '3:30') is the natural way to say the half hour, more idiomatic than spelling it out as さんじさんじゅっぷん (sanji sanjuppun) with ふん/ぷん (fun/pun).
Marks an ending point in time or place ('until'); pairs with から (kara, 'from') to state a range, as in しごとはくじからごじまでです (shigoto wa kuji kara goji made desu), 'work is from 9:00 to 5:00.'
Katakana loanword from English 'last order' - the deadline for placing a food or drink order before a restaurant's kitchen or bar closes, often stated with まで (made, 'until').

items.note: Uses く (ku), not きゅう (kyuu) from Lesson 2's number card - 9:00 is an irregular hour reading; most hours simply add じ (ji) to the cardinal number, as in はちじ (hachiji, 8:00).

items.target: しごとはくじからごじまでです
items.pronunciation: shigoto wa ku-ji kara go-ji made desu.

items.note: Uses よ (yo), not よん (yon) from Lesson 2's number card - 4:00 is an irregular hour reading; most hours simply add じ (ji) to the cardinal number, as in ろくじ (rokuji, 6:00).

items.target: かいぎはあしたのよじからです
items.pronunciation: kaigi wa ashita no yo-ji kara desu.
items.note: あしたの (ashita no) links two time expressions - 'tomorrow's 4:00' - extending の (no) beyond marking possession/affiliation, as in のぞみデパートのたなかさん (Nozomi Depaato no Tanaka-san) from Lesson 1, to connect a day to a specific time within it.
ひる (hiru) means 'noon' on its own (sub-entry under ひるやすみ (hiruyasumi), lunch break)
やすみ (yasumi) means 'break/time off' on its own (sub-entry under ひるやすみ (hiruyasumi), lunch break)
Uses しち (shichi), not なな (nana) from Lesson 2's number card - 7:00 keeps an older reading of 7 instead of the everyday cardinal number used elsewhere.

items.note: Suffix — attaches after a number to form the hour (written 〜じ (ji) in the source)

items.reviewNote: Possibly premature — explicitly re-taught later in Lesson 20: Going Places (3): How Do You Go There?, as a dedicated WORD POWER 'Periods' vocabulary entry (〜ふん／ぷん(かん)) in the duration sense, distinct from ch17's clock-time sense
items.note: Suffix — attaches after a number to form minutes; alternates between ふん (fun) and ぷん (pun) depending on the preceding sound (written 〜ふん (fun)／ぷん (pun) in the source)
ごぜん (gozen, 'A.M.') precedes the hour to disambiguate a 12-hour time, e.g. ごぜんよじ (gozen yoji), '4:00 A.M.' — paired with ごご (gogo, 'P.M.') for afternoon/evening hours.
ごご (gogo, 'P.M.') precedes the hour to disambiguate a 12-hour time, e.g. ごごくじ (gogo kuji), '9:00 P.M.' — paired with ごぜん (gozen, 'A.M.') for morning hours.
いつ (itsu, 'when') asks broadly about a date or time, e.g. パーティーはいつですか (paatii wa itsu desu ka), 'when is the party?' — contrast なんじ (nanji, 'what time'), which asks specifically for a clock hour.
あさ (asa) means 'morning' on its own (sub-entry under あさごはん (asagohan), breakfast)
ごはん (gohan) means 'meal/cooked rice' on its own (sub-entry under あさごはん (asagohan), breakfast)
Used specifically for a hotel's front desk (from English 'front'); うけつけ (uketsuke) is the more general word for a reception desk elsewhere.
ばん (ban) means 'evening' on its own (sub-entry under ばんごはん (bangohan), dinner)

Comments on what someone just told you, rather than confirming your own statement like そうです (sou desu) does. Falling intonation = 'I see' (acknowledging what you heard); rising intonation = 'Is that so? / Really?' (a genuine question).

どうも (doumo) adds emphasis ("thanks a lot"). This plain どうもありがとう (doumo arigatou) is warm but casual — fine for friendly, everyday thanks (e.g. to shop staff). Use the more formal ありがとうございます (arigatou gozaimasu) in polite or business settings; combine them as どうもありがとうございます (doumo arigatou gozaimasu) to be extra polite.
